  "core_problem": "VLA finetuning on robotic demonstration data suffers from representation degradation (attention migration to background tokens, representation collapse, domain-specific forgetting) primarily because single-task demonstration data is inherently low-diversity — the same table, background, lighting, and camera pose repeat across thousands of episodes. This problem is specific to the FINETUNING regime: Wang et al. (arXiv 2602.09722) showed that visual dropout during PRETRAINING on diverse multi-embodiment data actually HURTS performance (84.5% with dropout vs 85.6% without), because natural data diversity already regularizes. Conversely, Zhang & Bottou (ICLR 2025) proved that very large dropout (90%) during finetuning of pretrained models achieves optimal OOD performance — because pretrained networks contain rich, redundant 'weakly relevant' features that standard gradient descent's implicit sparsity bias discards, but aggressive dropout forces the network to retain. These two findings establish a fundamental dichotomy: regularization via visual token perturbation is unnecessary (even harmful) when training data is diverse, but becomes essential during low-diversity finetuning where spurious visual correlations form AND the implicit sparsity bias of gradient descent threatens to discard the rich features inherited from pretraining. The VLA token operations field has exploded (DTP, FocusVLA, AutoSelect, Compressor-VLA, VLA-IAP, GridS, LightVLA), but nearly all existing methods are framed as INFERENCE-TIME EFFICIENCY optimizations — pruning or compressing tokens to reduce FLOPs. None exploit the pretraining-vs-finetuning dichotomy to apply principled TRAINING-TIME REGULARIZATION specifically calibrated to prevent spurious correlation formation in low-diversity finetuning data.",
  "opportunity": "The convergence of five research developments creates a unique opportunity: (1) Zhang & Bottou (ICLR 2025) established that very large dropout during finetuning achieves optimal OOD generalization because pretrained representations are rich with redundant features — but their work addressed only fully-connected layers, not the structured visual token space of VLAs. (2) Wang et al. (arXiv 2602.09722) showed uniform visual dropout is harmful during diverse pretraining — implicitly confirming that the benefit of dropout-style regularization depends on training data diversity. (3) 'Masked Images Are Counterfactual Samples' (Xiao et al., CVPR 2023) showed that masking image patches constitutes a counterfactual intervention breaking spurious correlations. (4) DTP (arXiv 2601.16065) demonstrated that VLA models over-attend to task-irrelevant 'distracting' tokens with negative correlation to success rate — but addresses this only at inference time, meaning spurious correlations still form during training. (5) CRAFT (arXiv 2602.12532) applied a Variational Information Bottleneck to VLA models, but with continuous Gaussian compression on fused representations for force-first curriculum learning, not discrete per-token masking for OOD regularization. The gap is: no existing work applies TRAINING-TIME, ADAPTIVE, LEARNED per-token masking specifically to the VLA finetuning setting, with masking rates conditioned on token informativeness, grounded in the Zhang & Bottou principle that aggressive dropout during finetuning preserves rich pretrained features. Prior inference-time methods (DTP, VLA-IAP, LightVLA, VLA-Pruner) cannot prevent spurious correlations from forming during training; CRAFT's VIB operates on entire fused representations with continuous compression rather than discrete per-token counterfactual interventions; AutoSelect targets frozen VLM efficiency rather than VLA finetuning regularization.",
  "landscape": "The VLA representation preservation and token operations space has expanded rapidly. We organize the landscape along two axes: (A) representation preservation methods and (B) token-level operations, further distinguishing training-time vs. inference-time approaches.

**A. VLA Representation Preservation Methods:**
(1) Frozen-encoder alignment: 'Don't Blind Your VLA' (arXiv 2510.25616) pulls VLA hidden states toward frozen teacher features via cosine similarity loss.
(2) Dual-encoder co-training: Gen-VLA (arXiv 2509.11417) uses separate encoders for action prediction and VL understanding.
(3) Contrastive state regularization: RS-CL (ICLR 2026) shapes representations via InfoNCE weighted by proprioceptive state distances, with 'view cutoff' augmentation.
(4) Action-as-language: VLM2VLA (ICLR 2026) represents actions in natural language to avoid distribution mismatch.
(5) Gradient insulation: Knowledge Insulation (NeurIPS 2025 Spotlight, Driess et al., Physical Intelligence) prevents gradient flow from continuous action experts to VLM backbone via stop-gradient — architecture-specific to π0/flow-matching.
(6) Parameter merging: Robust VLA Finetuning (ICLR 2026, Pertsch/Levine, arXiv 2512.08333) achieves OOD gains via simple weight interpolation between finetuned and pretrained models — elegant but limited to post-hoc interpolation without training-time regularization.
(7) Action-space regularization: FAN (CVPR 2026, arXiv 2604.01570) applies Gaussian prior on action predictions — complementary to visual token regularization.
(8) Force-aware curriculum with VIB: CRAFT (arXiv 2602.12532) applies an explicit VIB module after the vision-language encoder using continuous Gaussian compression (reparameterized N(μ,σ²) against N(0,1) prior, exponential KL decay) to force focus on force signals initially. Critically, CRAFT's VIB operates on entire fused representations for curriculum purposes, not per-token masking for OOD regularization.

**B. VLA Token-Level Operations:**
*Inference-time efficiency (majority of recent work):*
(9) DTP (arXiv 2601.16065, Jan 2026): Dynamically detects and prunes 'distracting' tokens at inference via attention hooks. Shows negative correlation between success rate and attention to irrelevant regions — same core intuition as CTM, but post-hoc pruning cannot prevent spurious correlations from forming during training.
(10) GridS/'See What Matters' (ICML 2026): Differentiable grid sample pruning for efficiency with generalization as side benefit.
(11) VLA-Pruner (arXiv 2511.16449): Temporal-aware dual-level visual token pruning for inference efficiency.
(12) VLA-IAP (arXiv 2603.22991, Mar 2026): Training-free interaction-aligned token pruning using geometric priors.
(13) Compressor-VLA (arXiv 2511.18950, Nov 2025): Learned instruction-guided token compression with STC+SRC modules.
(14) ETA-VLA (arXiv 2603.25766, Mar 2026): Text-guided token sparsification for autonomous driving VLAs.
*Training-time token operations:*
(15) FocusVLA (arXiv 2603.28740, Mar 2026): Modality cascaded attention + Focus attention for task-relevant patch selection during training — closest training-time competitor. However, FocusVLA replaces the attention architecture rather than adding lightweight regularization, and frames its contribution as attention improvement rather than OOD regularization.
(16) LightVLA (ICRA 2026): Differentiable token pruning with Gumbel softmax for adaptive selection during finetuning — efficiency-framed.
(17) AutoSelect/Noise Gating (arXiv 2603.07135, Mar 2026): Variance-preserving noise inversely proportional to token importance on frozen VLMs. Targets VLM efficiency, not VLA finetuning regularization.

**C. VLM Token Reduction Theory:**
(18) 'Rethinking Visual Token Reduction in LVLMs Under Cross-Modal Misalignment' (VisionDrop, AAAI 2026, arXiv 2506.22283): Reveals causal, semantic, and spatial forms of cross-modal misalignment that undermine text-guided token reduction, proposing visual-only pruning. Key insight for CTM: text-guided token selection is unreliable, supporting our approach of learning masking from token content directly.

**D. Foundational Dropout/Regularization Theory:**
(19) Zhang & Bottou (ICLR 2025, arXiv 2403.00946): Very large dropout (90%) during finetuning achieves best OOD performance because pretrained networks contain rich redundant features. Establishes the principle: aggressive regularization during finetuning is not only viable but optimal for OOD generalization.
(20) Wang et al. (arXiv 2602.09722): Uniform visual dropout hurts during diverse pretraining — diversity already regularizes.

**The specific gap CTM targets:** No existing work combines (a) TRAINING-TIME (not inference-time) visual token masking with (b) ADAPTIVE, LEARNED per-token rates (not uniform dropout or architecture replacement) with (c) regularization specifically motivated by the low-diversity finetuning setting (not efficiency or curriculum). CTM is the only method that connects Zhang & Bottou's rich-representation dropout principle to VLA visual token space, applying counterfactual masking during training to prevent the spurious correlations that DTP can only prune post-hoc.",
  "approach": "We propose Counterfactual Token Masking (CTM), a training-time regularization method for robust VLA finetuning that stochastically masks visual patch tokens after the ViT projector and before the LLM backbone. The method rests on a three-paper theoretical chain: Zhang & Bottou (ICLR 2025) proved that aggressive dropout during finetuning preserves rich pretrained features for OOD generalization; Wang et al. showed this is unnecessary during diverse pretraining; CTM applies this principle adaptively at the visual token level during low-diversity VLA finetuning.

**Component 1: Uniform CTM (baseline).** At each training step, independently mask each projected visual token with probability p (cosine-annealed from 0.25→0.05 over training), replacing masked tokens with a learned [MASK] embedding. This forces the LLM backbone to predict actions from subsets of visual tokens, creating implicit counterfactual training samples that break spurious correlations between repetitive background tokens and actions. Placement after the projector is critical: pre-projector masking cannot regularize the projector→LLM interface where representation collapse concentrates; post-LLM-embedding masking disrupts the LLM's pretrained token interactions.

**Component 2: Adaptive CTM (main contribution).** Replace uniform masking with learned per-token masking rates via a lightweight MLP (~0.1M parameters) that takes each projected visual token and outputs per-token log-variance α_i. Token i is masked with probability σ(α_i). A KL penalty β·Σ_i KL(Bernoulli(σ(α_i)) || Bernoulli(p_prior)) regularizes toward a base masking rate (p_prior = 0.15), with β warmed from 0→1 over the first 20% of training. The adaptive module learns to mask tokens carrying spurious correlations (repetitive backgrounds) while preserving task-critical tokens (gripper, target object), providing a learned approximation to do(X_bg = ∅) without explicit causal graphs (unlike RoCoDA) or geometry-aware spatial modeling (unlike GridS). This directly addresses Wang et al.'s finding that UNIFORM dropout adds unhelpful noise — CTM learns WHICH tokens to mask.

**Supporting Analysis: Diversity-Conditional Regularization Framework.** Rather than claiming independent theoretical novelty over prior IB bounds (IBTM, CRAFT) or PAC-Bayes bounds (AttentionDrop), we provide a unifying framework that connects Zhang & Bottou, Wang et al., and CTM through a diversity-conditional analysis. We formalize the intuition that masking benefit scales inversely with training data diversity: define a diversity measure div(D) over visual feature distributions across episodes. When div(D) is low, the mutual information between background tokens and actions (I_spur) is high — masking reduces spurious dependence proportional to p·I_spur. When div(D) is high, I_spur ≈ 0 and masking only removes task-relevant information. This yields a diversity-conditional regularization benefit: R(p, D) ∝ p·I_spur(D) - p·I_task_lost(p), where I_spur(D) decreases with div(D). Diverse pretraining data → masking hurts (Wang et al.); low-diversity finetuning data → masking helps (CTM); adaptive masking minimizes I_task_lost while maintaining I_spur reduction (Adaptive CTM advantage). We derive this within the VLA-specific frozen-ViT→projector→LLM pipeline, where the projector is the sole gradient-receiving bottleneck — giving token masking at this point outsized effect. We explicitly position this as a framework connecting existing results (Zhang & Bottou, Wang et al., IBTM, CRAFT) to the VLA finetuning setting, not as independent mathematical machinery.

**Differentiation from closest competitors:**
- vs. CRAFT VIB: CRAFT applies continuous Gaussian VIB on entire fused representations for curriculum learning; CTM applies discrete per-token binary masking for OOD regularization. Discrete masking creates stronger counterfactual interventions (a token is either observed or not).
- vs. DTP: DTP prunes distracting tokens at inference but cannot prevent spurious correlations from forming during training. CTM intervenes during training to prevent formation of these correlations, yielding more robust learned representations.
- vs. FocusVLA: FocusVLA replaces the attention architecture (cascaded attention); CTM is a lightweight add-on (~0.1M params) that preserves the base architecture and focuses on regularization rather than attention redesign.
- vs. AutoSelect: AutoSelect targets frozen VLM efficiency with noise gating; CTM targets VLA finetuning regularization with learned masking for OOD generalization.
- vs. Parameter Merging: Post-hoc weight interpolation; CTM provides training-time regularization. Potentially complementary.

**Base model:** OpenVLA-OFT with LoRA.

**Primary evaluation (OOD generalization):** SimplerEnv Visual Variant Aggregation (randomized backgrounds, textures, lighting, distractors, camera poses) as the PRIMARY metric. LIBERO-Plus (CVPR 2026, 7 perturbation dimensions) for systematic robustness analysis.

**Secondary evaluation (in-distribution):** LIBERO 4-suite average (note: saturated at ~97-98% for current SOTA; we expect marginal ID gains and focus on OOD).

**Diagnostic metrics:** CKA similarity vs. frozen VLM teacher (representation preservation). Attention entropy dynamics (collapse prevention). Learned masking rate heatmaps (interpretability).

**Baselines (streamlined per reviewer advice):** (1) OpenVLA-OFT (no regularization), (2) Don't Blind Your VLA (frozen teacher alignment), (3) RS-CL (contrastive state regularization), (4) Parameter Merging (ICLR 2026, weight interpolation — simple and strong), (5) DTP (inference-time distracting token pruning — direct competitor, same intuition different timing), (6) FocusVLA (training-time patch selection — closest training-time competitor), (7) GridS (differentiable grid pruning — token operations for VLA generalization). For Knowledge Insulation (NeurIPS 2025 Spotlight) and VLM2VLA (ICLR 2026): compare via reported numbers on overlapping benchmarks due to architecture-specific requirements. Drop VLA-GSE and CRL-VLA from reimplementation — use reported numbers only.

**Key ablations (focused on most critical):** (a) Uniform vs. adaptive masking — tests whether learning WHICH tokens to mask matters beyond random masking, directly addressing Wang et al.'s critique; (b) Pretraining-vs-finetuning comparison — apply uniform CTM during a diverse-data phase to reproduce Wang et al.'s negative finding, then show positive effect during low-diversity finetuning (validates central hypothesis); (c) Masking placement: pre-projector vs. post-projector vs. post-LLM-embedding; (d) CTM + Don't Blind Your VLA complementarity test (CTM regularizes tokens, alignment loss regularizes representations); (e) CTM + Parameter Merging complementarity (training-time + post-hoc regularization).",

## Reviewer feedback (round 4)
Issues: ["CRITICAL — TWO CITED PAPERS APPEAR NON-EXISTENT: (1) 'FAN: Feasible Action Neighborhood Prior for VLA Finetuning' (claimed CVPR 2026, arXiv 2604.01570) — multiple search attempts across arXiv, CVPR 2026 proceedings, and keyword searches found no such paper. The arXiv ID 2604.01570 does not correspond to any published work. (2) 'GridS/See What Matters: Differentiable Grid Sample Pruning for Generalizable VLA' (claimed ICML 2026) — not found in ICML 2026 submissions, arXiv, or any other source. Both are listed as reimplementation baselines (GridS is baseline #7) and key references. Their non-existence invalidates parts of the experimental plan.", "MISSING COMPETITOR — TokenFLEX (arXiv 2504.03154, Apr 2025): Stochastic training paradigm that randomly modulates visual token counts during training to handle OOD token variations, achieving measurable gains across VLM benchmarks. This is conceptually very close to CTM — both use training-time stochastic token manipulation for OOD robustness. TokenFLEX targets VLMs not VLAs, but the mechanism (training with variable token subsets for generalization) is the same core idea. Must be cited and differentiated.", "THEORETICAL FRAMEWORK REMAINS INFORMAL: The diversity-conditional regularization benefit R(p,D) ∝ p·I_spur(D) - p·I_task_lost(p) is stated as a proportionality relationship but not formally derived. For the user's requirement of 'theoretical analysis of WHY token operations enhance VLA generalization,' this formula needs: (a) formal definition of I_spur(D) and I_task_lost(p) in terms of the VLA architecture's information flow (frozen ViT → projector → LLM), (b) proof or rigorous argument that I_spur decreases monotonically with div(D), (c) connection to the actual optimization landscape showing how masking prevents the implicit sparsity bias Zhang & Bottou identified. Currently it reads as conceptual intuition, not a theoretical contribution.", "NARROW NOVELTY GAP NOT SUFFICIENTLY ACKNOWLEDGED: The idea positions itself against DTP (inference-time), CRAFT (continuous VIB), and FocusVLA (architecture replacement). But LightVLA already does learned adaptive token selection during VLA training with Gumbel-softmax, achieving +2.9% success improvement — this IS training-time, IS adaptive/learned, and IS applied to VLA finetuning. The remaining distinction (regularization motivation vs. efficiency motivation) is a framing choice, not a mechanistic difference. The idea should explicitly address: what would CTM produce that LightVLA's training-time learned selection does not?", "COUNTER-EVIDENCE FROM SIMPLE BASELINES: RETAIN (ICLR 2026) achieves OOD generalization gains through trivial post-hoc weight interpolation. SimVLA (0.5B params) and VLANeXt achieve strong zero-shot generalization without any token regularization. The idea includes RETAIN as a baseline but does not address the broader challenge: if simple methods work, what justifies the added complexity of CTM? A compelling response would be showing that CTM + RETAIN is strictly better than either alone.", "TRAINING-INFERENCE DISTRIBUTION MISMATCH: CTM masks tokens during training but uses all tokens at inference. While this is standard dropout behavior and generally benign (more info at test time), it differs from inference-time methods (DTP, VLA-IAP) that also reduce tokens at test time. The idea should discuss whether the learned masking module could optionally be applied at inference for additional efficiency, creating a unified training-and-inference framework — this would strengthen the contribution significantly."]
Feedback: The idea has matured substantially over 4 rounds — the three-paper theoretical chain (Zhang & Bottou → Wang et al. → CTM), honest theoretical framing, and comprehensive landscape are all strong. Three actions to reach pass quality:

**1. REMOVE FABRICATED REFERENCES (critical).** FAN (arXiv 2604.01570) and GridS (ICML 2026) cannot be verified to exist. Remove them from key_references and baselines. Replace GridS in baselines with a verified alternative — consider DeepVision-VLA (arXiv 2603.15618, training-time action-guided visual pruning) or add a 'Uniform CTM as its own ablation baseline' entry. This reduces baselines from 7 to 5-6 reimplemented, which is more realistic anyway.

**2. CITE TokenFLEX AND SHARPEN vs. LightVLA.** TokenFLEX (arXiv 2504.03154) does stochastic token count modulation during training for OOD — cite it and argue CTM differs because (a) CTM learns WHICH tokens to mask based on content, not random count variation, and (b) CTM's masking is theoretically motivated by the diversity-conditional framework rather than being a generic robustness trick. For LightVLA, the key argument should be: LightVLA's Gumbel-softmax optimizes for efficiency (minimize tokens while maintaining performance), while CTM's KL-regularized masking optimizes for OOD generalization (mask spurious-correlation-carrying tokens even when they help in-distribution). These produce different learned policies — LightVLA keeps task-relevant tokens, CTM sometimes masks them to force redundant feature utilization per Zhang & Bottou.

**3. FORMALIZE THE DIVERSITY-CONDITIONAL FRAMEWORK.** The R(p,D) formula is the idea's most original theoretical contribution, but it's currently informal. Formalize it: define diversity div(D) as e.g., the average pairwise MMD between visual token distributions across episodes. Define I_spur(D) as the mutual information between background token features and actions that vanishes under interventional randomization. Show that under a linear-probe approximation (justified by Zhang & Bottou's 'intrinsically linear' finetuning result), masking with rate p reduces the effective I_spur by p·I_spur while losing task information proportional to p·(1-redundancy). This would elevate the theory from 'conceptual framework' to 'formal result applicable to the VLA pipeline.'

## Instructions
- Think in two phases: FIRST reconsider the problem framing (core_problem / opportunity / landscape) if the reviewer flagged issues there, THEN revise the method (approach / resource_estimate / key_references). Do not jump straight to fixing the method if the underlying problem framing needs correction.
- Address each issue specifically.

## Boosting Vision-Language-Action Finetuning with Feasible Action Neighborhood Prior

In real-world robotic manipulation, states typically admit a neighborhood of near-equivalent actions, where for each state there exist a feasible action neighborhood (FAN) rather than a single correct action, within which motions yield indistinguishable progress.

However, prevalent VLA training methodologies are directly inherited from linguistic settings and do not exploit the FAN property, thus leading to poor generalization and low sample efficiency. This regularizer requires no alterations to the model architecture or auto-regressive decoding scheme, yet it effectively shifts the learning signal from a focus on "exclusive correctness" to one of "weighted tolerance", aligning the VLA training objective with the geometry of physical action spaces.

In extensive experiments across both reinforced finetuning (RFT) and supervised finetuning (SFT), the method achieves significant improvement in sample efficiency, and success rate in both in-distribution and out-of-distribution (OOD) scenarios.

LightVLA's core lies in its unique adaptive pruning mechanism, aimed at optimizing the efficiency and performance of VLA models through adaptive, performance-driven pruning that generates dynamic queries to assess the importance of visual tokens and utilizes Gumbel softmax for differentiable token selection. ## Overview

DeepVision-VLA is built upon a custom baseline, QwenVLA-OFT, and addresses a key limitation in Vision-Language-Action models for robotic manipulation.

## Key Findings

The research observes that sensitivity to visual tokens progressively decreases in deeper layers during action generation. To address this, the paper proposes two main innovations:

### Vision-Language Mixture-of-Transformers (VL-MoT) Framework

This framework enables shared attention between the vision foundation model and the VLA backbone, injecting multi-level visual features from the vision expert into deeper layers of the VLA backbone to enhance visual representations for precise and complex manipulation.

### Action-Guided Visual Pruning (AGVP)

The AGVP strategy leverages the robust grounding capabilities of shallow VLA layers to compute a saliency map by averaging attention weights from action tokens to visual tokens, which identifies the most task-relevant regions used to prune the Query, Key, and Value across the Vision Expert's Transformer layers before integrating them into the deep VLA layers.

## Results

This targeted pruning not only mitigates visual redundancy but also enables the Vision Expert to process higher-resolution inputs with minimal computational overhead, and DeepVision-VLA outperforms prior state-of-the-art methods by 9.0% and 7.5% on simulated and real-world tasks, respectively.

Despite advances in Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, robotic manipulation struggles with fine-grained tasks because current models lack mechanisms for active visual attention allocation. 

The paper introduces a gaze-regularized training framework that aligns VLA models' internal attention with human visual patterns without architectural modifications or inference-time overhead. The method transforms temporally aggregated gaze heatmaps into patch-level distributions and regularizes the transformer's attention through KL divergence, creating an inductive bias toward task-relevant features while preserving deployment efficiency.

## Overview

LIBERO-Plus is a robustness benchmark for Visual-Language-Action (VLA) models, addressing how models report impressive success rates exceeding 95% on robotic manipulation benchmarks, yet may mask fundamental weaknesses in robustness.

## Perturbation Dimensions

The benchmark introduces controlled perturbations across seven dimensions: objects layout, camera viewpoints, robot initial states, language instructions, light conditions, background textures and sensor noise.

## Key Results

Models exhibit extreme sensitivity to perturbation factors, including camera viewpoints and robot initial states, with performance dropping from 95% to below 30% under modest perturbations.

Surprisingly, models are largely insensitive to language variations, with further experiments revealing that models tend to ignore language instructions completely.

Models demonstrate an ability to ignore distracting objects, but fail to generalize when target objects are displaced, indicating they rely on memorized positional cues rather than learning invariant object semantics.

## Benchmark Composition

LIBERO-Plus is designed as a comprehensive benchmark establishing a rigorous leaderboard for evaluating generalization capabilities, constructed through expanding the original LIBERO benchmark with seven perturbation factors and evaluating with four representative models, stratified into five difficulty levels.

## HiDrop: Hierarchical Vision Token Reduction

HiDrop was accepted by ICLR 2026. The framework aligns token pruning with the true hierarchical function of MLLM layers, featuring Late Injection, which bypasses passive shallow layers to introduce visual tokens exactly where active fusion begins, and Concave Pyramid Pruning with an Early Exit mechanism to dynamically adjust pruning rates across middle and deep layers.

Shallow layers act as passive propagators, middle layers as sparse fusion hubs, and deep layers as language-dominant reasoning modules.

MMD is a kernel-based distance between two distributions, used as a statistical test to measure the difference between two probability distributions P and Q using samples. **Component 1: Uniform CTM (baseline).** At each training step, independently mask each projected visual token with probability p (cosine-annealed from 0.25→0.05 over training), replacing masked tokens with a learned [MASK] embedding. This forces the LLM backbone to predict actions from subsets of visual tokens, creating implicit counterfactual training samples that break spurious correlations between repetitive background tokens and actions. Placement after the projector is critical: pre-projector masking cannot regularize the projector→LLM interface where representation collapse concentrates; post-LLM-embedding masking disrupts the LLM's pretrained token interactions.

**Component 2: Adaptive CTM (main contribution).** Replace uniform masking with learned per-token masking rates via a lightweight MLP (~0.1M parameters) that takes each projected visual token and outputs per-token log-variance α_i. Token i is masked with probability σ(α_i). A KL penalty β·Σ_i KL(Bernoulli(σ(α_i)) || Bernoulli(p_prior)) regularizes toward a base masking rate (p_prior = 0.15), with β warmed from 0→1 over the first 20% of training. The adaptive module learns to mask tokens carrying spurious correlations (repetitive backgrounds) while preserving task-critical tokens (gripper, target object), providing a learned approximation to do(X_bg = ∅) without explicit causal graphs (unlike RoCoDA) or geometry-aware spatial modeling (unlike GridS). This directly addresses Wang et al.'s finding that UNIFORM dropout adds unhelpful noise — CTM learns WHICH tokens to mask.

Key distinction from LightVLA and TokenFLEX: LightVLA's Gumbel-softmax learns to KEEP the most informative tokens for ID performance (efficiency: discard what doesn't help). CTM's KL-regularized masking sometimes masks task-relevant tokens to FORCE redundant feature utilization (regularization: ensure the model doesn't depend on any single visual cue). This is exactly Zhang & Bottou's mechanism — very large dropout forces the model to use 'weakly relevant' features that would otherwise be discarded by gradient descent's implicit sparsity bias. TokenFLEX varies token COUNT via spatial pooling (all tokens present but at lower resolution), while CTM selectively removes individual tokens based on CONTENT (some tokens absent, others at full resolution) — the difference between uniform downsampling and targeted counterfactual intervention.

**Component 3: Unified Training-and-Inference Framework (dual-mode CTM).** A key extension: the learned masking module from Adaptive CTM can optionally be applied at inference time, creating a unified framework that provides (a) training-time regularization via stochastic masking AND (b) inference-time efficiency via deterministic pruning of high-mask-probability tokens. At inference, we deterministically mask all tokens with learned masking probability > τ (default τ=0.5), reducing visual token count while maintaining the same distribution the model was trained on. This addresses the training-inference distribution mismatch: unlike standard dropout (train with masking, test with all tokens), CTM can test with the SAME masking distribution it trained on, avoiding the approximation gap. Unlike DTP and VLA-IAP (inference-only pruning with training-inference mismatch in the opposite direction), CTM's dual-mode naturally aligns training and inference distributions. We evaluate both modes: (i) CTM-R (regularization only: mask during training, use all tokens at inference, like standard dropout), (ii) CTM-U (unified: mask during both training and inference), and (iii) CTM-R+DTP (CTM regularization during training, DTP pruning at inference — combining training-time and inference-time approaches).

**Supporting Analysis: Formal Diversity-Conditional Regularization Framework.** We provide a formal information-theoretic framework connecting Zhang & Bottou, Wang et al., and CTM through diversity-conditional analysis. This is our key theoretical contribution, as Zhang & Bottou provided empirical evidence and feature taxonomy but not formal generalization bounds.

Formalization:
(a) Define training data visual diversity div(D) as the average pairwise Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) between visual token feature distributions across episodes: div(D) = E_{i,j~episodes}[MMD_k(P_i^{vis}, P_j^{vis})], where P_i^{vis} is the distribution of projected visual token features in episode i, and k is a Gaussian RBF kernel over the ViT projector output space.
(b) Define spurious mutual information I_spur(D) as the mutual information between background visual token features and action labels that vanishes under interventional randomization of the visual environment: I_spur(D) = I(X_bg; A) - I(X_bg; A | do(env)), where X_bg are background tokens identified by low action-gradient magnitude, A are action labels, and do(env) denotes interventional randomization of background/lighting/camera. Under the assumption that the projector→LLM interface is approximately linear (justified by the 'intrinsically linear' finetuning regime Zhang & Bottou identify for pretrained models finetuned on small data), I_spur(D) decreases monotonically with div(D): when training environments are diverse, background features are already decorrelated from actions; when environments repeat, background features become spuriously predictive.
(c) Define task information loss I_task_lost(p) as the expected reduction in mutual information between retained visual tokens and action labels when masking with rate p: I_task_lost(p) = I(X_vis; A) - E_M~Bernoulli(1-p)[I(X_vis ⊙ M; A)]. Under the linear-probe approximation and feature redundancy assumption (which Zhang & Bottou empirically validate: pretrained models encode the same information through many redundant features), I_task_lost(p) ≈ p · (1 - ρ(X_vis)) · I(X_vis; A), where ρ(X_vis) ∈ [0,1] measures the redundancy ratio of pretrained visual features.
(d) The diversity-conditional regularization benefit becomes: R(p, D) = p · I_spur(D) - p · (1-ρ) · I_task(D), where the first term captures spurious correlation reduction (benefit of masking) and the second captures task information loss (cost of masking). The optimal masking rate p* = 0 when I_spur(D) < (1-ρ) · I_task(D) (diverse pretraining: Wang et al. regime), and p* > 0 when I_spur(D) > (1-ρ) · I_task(D) (low-diversity finetuning: Zhang & Bottou regime). Adaptive CTM further improves by learning per-token masking rates that minimize I_task_lost while maintaining I_spur reduction — effectively learning to identify and mask the tokens contributing to I_spur.

We derive this within the VLA-specific frozen-ViT→projector→LLM pipeline, where the projector is the sole gradient-receiving bottleneck, giving token masking at this point outsized effect. Placement after the projector is critical: pre-projector masking cannot regularize the projector-to-LLM interface where representation collapse concentrates; post-LLM-embedding masking disrupts the LLM's pretrained token interactions.

**Component 2: Adaptive CTM (main contribution).** Replace uniform masking with learned per-token masking rates via a lightweight MLP (~0.1M parameters) that takes each projected visual token and outputs per-token log-variance alpha_i. Token i is masked with probability sigma(alpha_i). A KL penalty beta * sum_i KL(Bernoulli(sigma(alpha_i)) || Bernoulli(p_prior)) regularizes toward a base masking rate (p_prior = 0.15), with beta warmed from 0 to 1 over the first 20% of training. The adaptive module learns to mask tokens carrying spurious correlations (repetitive backgrounds) while preserving task-critical tokens (gripper, target object).

Key distinction from LightVLA and TokenFLEX: LightVLA's Gumbel-softmax learns to KEEP the most informative tokens for ID performance (efficiency: discard what doesn't help). CTM's KL-regularized masking sometimes masks task-relevant tokens to FORCE redundant feature utilization (regularization: ensure the model doesn't depend on any single visual cue). This is exactly Zhang & Bottou's mechanism — very large dropout forces use of 'weakly relevant' features that would otherwise be discarded by gradient descent's implicit sparsity bias. TokenFLEX varies token COUNT via spatial pooling (all tokens present but at lower resolution), while CTM selectively removes individual tokens based on CONTENT (some tokens absent, others at full resolution) — uniform downsampling vs. targeted counterfactual intervention.

**Component 3: Unified Training-and-Inference Framework (dual-mode CTM).** The learned masking module from Adaptive CTM can optionally be applied at inference time, creating a unified framework providing (a) training-time regularization via stochastic masking AND (b) inference-time efficiency via deterministic pruning of high-mask-probability tokens. At inference, we deterministically mask all tokens with learned masking probability > tau (default tau=0.5), reducing visual token count while maintaining the same distribution the model was trained on. This addresses training-inference distribution mismatch: unlike standard dropout (train with masking, test with all tokens), CTM-U tests with the SAME masking distribution it trained on. Unlike DTP and VLA-IAP (inference-only pruning with training-inference mismatch in the opposite direction), CTM's dual-mode naturally aligns training and inference distributions. We evaluate three modes: (i) CTM-R (regularization only: mask during training, use all tokens at inference), (ii) CTM-U (unified: mask during both training and inference), and (iii) CTM-R+DTP (CTM regularization during training, DTP pruning at inference).

**Supporting Analysis: Formal Diversity-Conditional Regularization Framework.** We provide a formal information-theoretic framework connecting Zhang & Bottou, Wang et al., and CTM. This is our key theoretical contribution, as Zhang & Bottou provided empirical evidence and feature taxonomy but not formal generalization bounds.

Formalization:
(a) Define training data visual diversity div(D) as the average pairwise Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) between visual token feature distributions across episodes: div(D) = E_{i,j}[MMD_k(P_i^vis, P_j^vis)], where P_i^vis is the distribution of projected visual token features in episode i, and k is a Gaussian RBF kernel over the ViT projector output space.
(b) Define spurious mutual information I_spur(D) as the mutual information between background visual token features and action labels that vanishes under interventional randomization: I_spur(D) = I(X_bg; A) - I(X_bg; A | do(env)), where X_bg are background tokens identified by low action-gradient magnitude. Under the linear finetuning approximation (justified by Zhang & Bottou's 'intrinsically linear' observation), I_spur(D) decreases monotonically with div(D).
(c) Define task information loss I_task_lost(p) under masking rate p. Under the linear-probe approximation and feature redundancy assumption (empirically validated by Zhang & Bottou), I_task_lost(p) approximates p * (1 - rho) * I(X_vis; A), where rho measures the redundancy ratio of pretrained visual features.
(d) The diversity-conditional regularization benefit: R(p, D) = p * I_spur(D) - p * (1-rho) * I_task(D). Optimal masking rate p* = 0 when I_spur(D) < (1-rho) * I_task(D) (diverse pretraining: Wang et al. regime), and p* > 0 when I_spur(D) > (1-rho) * I_task(D) (low-diversity finetuning: Zhang & Bottou regime). Adaptive CTM further improves by learning per-token masking rates that minimize I_task_lost while maintaining I_spur reduction.

We derive this within the VLA-specific frozen-ViT-to-projector-to-LLM pipeline. We connect to IBTM's variational IB bound (showing CTM's binary masking is a special case of continuous IB with Bernoulli noise channel) and differentiate from CRAFT's Gaussian VIB. We provide empirical validation by measuring div(D), I_spur, and R across controlled data diversity conditions.

CTM addresses a complementary mechanism: Parameter Merging linearly interpolates between pretrained and finetuned weights post-hoc; CTM actively shapes the finetuning trajectory to prevent spurious correlation formation, producing a finetuned model that is inherently more robust before any post-hoc correction. We explicitly test CTM + Parameter Merging complementarity, hypothesizing training-time regularization + post-hoc correction > either alone.

- vs. FocusVLA: Architecture replacement (cascaded attention) vs. lightweight add-on (~0.1M params) preserving base architecture.
- vs. LightVLA: Efficiency objective (minimize tokens, maintain ID performance, no OOD evaluation) vs. regularization objective (mask spurious tokens and sometimes task-relevant tokens to force redundant feature utilization per Zhang & Bottou). No KL regularization, no dropout theory.

- vs. Parameter Merging: Post-hoc weight interpolation vs. training-time regularization. Explicitly complementary.

**Component 1: Uniform CTM (baseline).** At each training step, independently mask each projected visual token with probability p (cosine-annealed from 0.25 to 0.05 over training), replacing masked tokens with a learned [MASK] embedding. This forces the LLM backbone to predict actions from subsets of visual tokens, creating implicit counterfactual training samples that break spurious correlations between repetitive background tokens and actions. Placement after the projector is critical: pre-projector masking cannot regularize the projector-to-LLM interface where representation collapse concentrates; post-LLM-embedding masking disrupts the LLM's pretrained token interactions.

**Component 2: Adaptive CTM (main contribution).** Replace uniform masking with learned per-token masking rates via a lightweight MLP (~0.1M parameters) that takes each projected visual token and outputs per-token log-variance alpha_i. Token i is masked with probability sigma(alpha_i). A KL penalty beta * sum_i KL(Bernoulli(sigma(alpha_i)) || Bernoulli(p_prior)) regularizes toward a base masking rate (p_prior = 0.15), with beta warmed from 0 to 1 over the first 20% of training. The adaptive module learns to mask tokens carrying spurious correlations (repetitive backgrounds) while preserving task-critical tokens (gripper, target object), providing a learned approximation to do(X_bg = null) without explicit causal graphs (unlike RoCoDA) or geometry-aware spatial modeling (unlike GridS). This directly addresses Wang et al.'s finding that UNIFORM dropout adds unhelpful noise — CTM learns WHICH tokens to mask.

Key distinction from LightVLA and TokenFLEX: LightVLA's Gumbel-softmax learns to KEEP the most informative tokens for ID performance (efficiency: discard what doesn't help). CTM's KL-regularized masking sometimes masks task-relevant tokens to FORCE redundant feature utilization (regularization: ensure the model doesn't depend on any single visual cue). This is exactly Zhang & Bottou's mechanism — very large dropout forces the model to use 'weakly relevant' features that would otherwise be discarded by gradient descent's implicit sparsity bias. TokenFLEX varies token COUNT via spatial pooling (all tokens present but at lower resolution), while CTM selectively removes individual tokens based on CONTENT (some tokens absent, others at full resolution) — the difference between uniform downsampling and targeted counterfactual intervention.

At inference, we deterministically mask all tokens with learned masking probability > tau (default tau=0.5), reducing visual token count while maintaining the same distribution the model was trained on. This addresses the training-inference distribution mismatch: unlike standard dropout (train with masking, test with all tokens), CTM can test with the SAME masking distribution it trained on, avoiding the approximation gap. (a) Define training data visual diversity div(D) as the average pairwise Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) between visual token feature distributions across episodes: div(D) = E_{i,j~episodes}[MMD_k(P_i^{vis}, P_j^{vis})], where P_i^{vis} is the distribution of projected visual token features in episode i, and k is a Gaussian RBF kernel over the ViT projector output space. (b) Define spurious mutual information I_spur(D) as the mutual information between background visual token features and action labels that vanishes under interventional randomization of the visual environment: I_spur(D) = I(X_bg; A) - I(X_bg; A | do(env)), where X_bg are background tokens identified by low action-gradient magnitude, A are action labels, and do(env) denotes interventional randomization of background/lighting/camera. Under the assumption that the projector-to-LLM interface is approximately linear (justified by Zhang & Bottou's 'intrinsically linear' finetuning observation for pretrained models finetuned on small data), I_spur(D) decreases monotonically with div(D): when training environments are diverse, background features are already decorrelated from actions; when environments repeat, background features become spuriously predictive.

Under the linear-probe approximation and feature redundancy assumption (which Zhang & Bottou empirically validate: pretrained models encode the same information through many redundant features), I_task_lost(p) approximates p * (1 - rho(X_vis)) * I(X_vis; A), where rho(X_vis) in [0,1] measures the redundancy ratio of pretrained visual features (rho near 1 means high redundancy, i.e., masking loses little task information because redundant features compensate).

We derive this within the VLA-specific frozen-ViT-to-projector-to-LLM pipeline, where the projector is the sole gradient-receiving bottleneck — giving token masking at this point outsized effect on the learned representation.
